$comment: What this repository contributes to a running stack, and what a check may
believe about it. `checked` is proved against this repository by
internal/manifest/manifest_test.go in this repository's own CI; `declared` is
a statement nobody can verify and carries its own `why`.
IT READS NO ENVIRONMENT AT ALL, AND THAT IS A CLAIM RATHER THAN AN ABSENCE.
Every other manifest in this estate lists variables and the test fails when
it finds none, on the grounds that finding none means the reader broke. Here
finding none is the truth: there is no QRYX_ name in any file, test files
included. So the claim is inverted and checked as such, and the day somebody
adds one, this goes red and the manifest has to say so.
THE EXIT CODES ARE THE OPPOSITE OF MOCKRYX'S, IN THE SAME ESTATE.
qryx scan   0 the scan completed, however much it found
1 a tool or usage error
2 findings, and only when --fail-on/--fail-on-new/--policy
asked for that
mockryx run 0 the drill ran and everything held
1 the drill ran and scenarios failed
2 refused for configuration
So 1 and 2 mean opposite kinds of thing in two tools a single routine file
calls, and a caller that assumed one convention would misread the other.
stack-up's routine gets this right and says why in a comment; nothing on this
side asserted it until now.
FINDINGS ALONE DO NOT CHANGE THE EXIT CODE. That is the part worth proving:
a scan of a file with three real findings exits 0 unless a flag asked
otherwise, so a caller reading 0 as `nothing found` would be wrong every
time.

the_cluster_pulls_a_published_image.why: Unlike most of this estate, qryx publishes an image and stack-k8s pulls it rather than building from source. Which tag a deployment pins is its decision and C1 already watches for a lag, so no version is claimed here.

the_routine_name_is_not_a_binary_name.why: estate.json's `runs` carries the ROUTINE's name. The binary is `qryx` and the routine is `qryx scan --save-evidence <dir> <path>`, which is why this component maps to a subcommand.
